textbook_items_in_class.description: Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object of the student's choice using a scale; record the measurements in centimetres using tenth notation as modelled in the section.

time_bands.activity: Open with Sonu's screw scenario: two screws look identical but differ by a fraction of a centimetre. Students examine a ruler and try to express a length such as 2 7/10 cm in their own words, articulating why whole-centimetre readings fail.

Students place a pen and a sharpener on a millimetre-ruled scale and record readings. Class discusses why the gap between two readings cannot be described using only whole centimetres — building the intuition that a smaller unit is necessary.

Figure it Out, section 3.1 p.47 ("Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object of the student's choice….") — students complete the measurement task independently, writing each length as a mixed number of centimetres and tenth-parts.
Whole-class share-out: students compare readings and identify cases where two objects differ by less than one centimetre, consolidating why the tenth-of-a-centimetre is a natural and necessary unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Ground the opening in the screw scenario from the section — the physical act of placing an object on a millimetre scale and noticing that the tip falls between two centimetre marks is exactly the motivating experience the section intends. Watch for students who record a length of, say, 7.3 cm as simply '7 cm' by rounding — ask them what they would lose if the competing screw measured 7.7 cm.
materials: millimetre-ruled rulers (one per student or pair)
a small classroom object of each student's choice

periods.activity_title: Building with Tenths: Mixed Numbers on the Ruler

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write lengths of objects (USB cable, and others shown in diagrams) in two ways — as a mixed number and as an improper tenth fraction — and read them aloud.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.49
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange eight lengths in increasing order: (a) 9/10; (b) 1 7/10; (c) 130/10; (d) 13 1/10; (e) 10 5/10; (f) 7 6/10; (g) 6 7/10; (h) 4/10.
Arrange four lengths in increasing order: 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10, 41 1/10.

time_bands.activity: Using the pencil-length diagram from the section, the teacher introduces the mixed number 3 4/10 and shows that 34 one-tenths equal three full units plus four tenths. Students draw this on a rough number line to see the decomposition.

Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.49 ("Write lengths of objects (USB cable, and others…) in two ways….") — students express each given length as both a mixed number and an improper fraction in tenths, then read each aloud to a partner.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.49 ("Arrange eight lengths in increasing order: (a) 9/10; (b) 1 7/10; (c) 130/10….") and Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.50 ("Arrange four lengths in increasing order: 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10, 41 1/10.") — pairs work through both ordering tasks, converting to a common form before comparing.

Quick class discussion: students articulate the rule they discovered for ordering tenth-fractions — is it easier to convert to improper fractions first, or to compare whole parts then tenth parts? Record the two strategies on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established through measurement that lengths fall between centimetre marks, this unit formalises the one-tenth as a named unit and asks students to move fluently between mixed-number and improper-fraction forms. A common error is converting 4 1/10 as 41/10 and then misreading 41 1/10 — remind students that the whole-number part must be multiplied by 10 before adding the tenths digit.
materials: pencil-length diagram (sketched or printed from textbook)

periods.activity_title: Adding and Subtracting Tenths in Two Ways

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total length of a honeybee given head = 2 3/10 units, thorax = 5 4/10 units, abdomen = 7 5/10 units.
Find the length of Shylaja's middle finger given total hand length 12 4/10 units and palm length 6 7/10 units; discuss two methods shown and try computing by converting to tenths.
Find the difference in lengths between a Celestial Pearl Danio (2 4/10 cm) and a Philippine Goby (9/10 cm); compare to finger size.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe six sequences of tenth-fractions, identify the change after each term, and extend each pattern by four more terms: (a) 4, 4 3/10, 4 6/10, …; (b) 8 2/10, 8 7/10, 9 2/10, …; (c) 7 6/10, 8 7/10, …; (d) 5 7/10, 5 3/10, …; (e) 13 5/10, 13, 12 5/10, …; (f) 11 5/10, 10 4/10, 9 3/10, …

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the two methods for addition from the section — 'units and tenths separately' and 'convert everything to tenths' — using the arm-length example (2 7/10 + 3 6/10). Students copy both side by side and verify they give the same result.

Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.51 ("Find the total length of a honeybee given head = 2 3/10….") and Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.51 ("Find the length of Shylaja's middle finger….") — students apply both methods to each problem and circle the method they found faster.

Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.52 ("Find the difference in lengths between a Celestial Pearl Danio (2 4/10 cm) and a Philippine Goby (9/10 cm)….") — students carry out the regrouping subtraction and compare the fish length to their own finger width.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.52 ("Observe six sequences of tenth-fractions, identify the change after each term….") — students work individually on the six sequences, identifying the constant step before extending. Pairs compare answers for the last three sequences.

periods.teacher_notes: The regrouping step in subtraction (borrowing one unit as 10 tenths) is the sharpest challenge here — students who avoid regrouping often subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position. For the sequences task, watch for students who correctly spot the step value but then apply it in the wrong direction on decreasing sequences.

periods.activity_title: Folding to Hundredths: A New Smaller Unit

textbook_items_in_class.description: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can the folded-paper length also be stated as 4 units and 45 one-hundredths? Explain.
Fill the empty boxes in the ruler diagram: given markings at 0, 1/10, 1/100, 2/10, 20/100, 1, 99/100, 130/100, 3/10, 2, identify the missing decimal lengths at each marked position.
For lengths shown in the diagrams, write each measurement in decimal fraction form and read the measurement aloud in words (sample answers: 5 37/100 and 15 3/100 shown in the teacher answer key).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55
textbook_items_in_class.description: In seven groups (a)–(g), identify the longest and shortest length from the given set of tenths and hundredths values, and mark each length on the scale.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-enacts the folded-paper problem: a strip of length 8 9/10 units folded in half gives a length that cannot be expressed in whole tenths alone. Students fold a strip of paper and measure the result, observing that it falls between two tenth marks.

Math Talk, section 3.3 p.53 ("How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can the folded-paper length also be stated as 4 units and 45 one-hundredths?….") — pairs discuss orally and then write a brief explanation, establishing that 10 hundredths = 1 tenth and 100 hundredths = 1 unit.

Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.54 ("Fill the empty boxes in the ruler diagram….") and Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.54 ("For lengths shown in the diagrams, write each measurement in decimal fraction form….") — students complete both ruler tasks, connecting the physical position of a mark to its mixed-fraction representation.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55 ("In seven groups (a)–(g), identify the longest and shortest length….") — students work through the seven groups, ordering mixed tenths-and-hundredths values and marking them on the scale diagram.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual move here is that one tenth decomposes into ten hundredths — students who understood the tenth as indivisible will need to see the folded paper physically landing between two tenth marks. A common confusion is treating 3/10 and 30/100 as different lengths; the ruler task at p.54 directly addresses this by labelling equivalent positions.
materials: strips of paper approximately 20 cm long (one per student)

periods.activity_title: Column Arithmetic with Tenths and Hundredths

textbook_items_in_class.description: Solve by converting to hundredths: find the difference 25 9/10 – 6 4/10 7/100; then find 15 3/10 4/100 – 2 6/10 8/100 and observe structural similarity with whole-number column subtraction 653 – 268.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.58

time_bands.activity: Math Talk, section 3.3 p.57 ("Solve by converting to hundredths: find the difference 25 9/10 – 6 4/10 7/100….") — teacher works through the first difference on the board using column-wise place value decomposition, explicitly labelling units, tenths, and hundredths columns. Students then solve the second subtraction independently and compare their working with the whole-number column subtraction 653 – 268.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.58 ("Find sums and differences of mixed tenths-and-hundredths numbers: (a) 3/10 + 4/100 + 3 4/100; (b) 9 5/10 7/100 + 2 1/10 3/100….") — students work through all six parts using whichever method they prefer (column decomposition or convert-to-hundredths), showing full working.

Pairs exchange books and check each other's answers for part (f), the most demanding subtraction involving regrouping across both the tenths and units columns. Class identifies any disagreement and resolves it at the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the hundredth as a unit in the previous sitting, this unit asks students to compute with mixed tenths-and-hundredths quantities — the structural analogy with whole-number column arithmetic is the section's central insight. Watch for students who align digits by position from the left rather than aligning the unit column; part (a), where there is no whole-number part, is a particular trap.

periods.activity_title: Why Ten? Extending Place Value into Decimals

textbook_items_in_class.description: Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator? What ambiguity arises? Show three different quantities that could all be denoted '705' without a positional separator.

How Big? Answer: (a) how many thousandths make one unit; (b) how many thousandths make one tenth; (c) how many thousandths make one hundredth; (d) how many tenths make one ten; (e) how many hundredths make one ten. Then make a few more similar questions and answer them.
Make a place value table (hundreds, tens, units, tenths, hundredths, thousandths). Write each quantity in decimal form, place value expansion, and read aloud.
Write in decimal form: (a) 234 hundredths; (b) 105 tenths.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the section's opening question: could we split a unit into 4 or 8 equal parts instead of 10? Students argue in pairs, then the class converges on the deductive reason: the Indian place value system is already organised in powers of 10, so splitting by 10 extends the same chain without breaking it.

Teacher draws the full place value chain (10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 → 1 → 1/10 → 1/100 → 1/1000) on the board. Math Talk, section 3.4 p.61 ("Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator? What ambiguity arises?….") — students identify three different quantities the string '705' could represent, articulating why a positional separator is essential.

Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.61 ("How Big? Answer: (a) how many thousandths make one unit….") and Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.63 ("Make a place value table….") — students complete both exercises, entering each given quantity into the table and writing the decimal form.

Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.64 ("Write in decimal form: (a) 234 hundredths; (b) 105 tenths.") — students solve these two conversion items using place value decomposition. Teacher then bridges to section 3.5 by asking: if 1 mm = 1/10 cm, what decimal does that give? The class derives 0.1 cm together before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The deductive thread here runs from the structure of the base-ten system to the necessity of the decimal point — students should leave able to articulate WHY the point is placed where it is, not merely follow a rule. A common error when converting '234 hundredths' is writing 234.00 rather than 2.34; emphasise that the place value table is the check, not estimation.
materials: ruler or board for drawing the place value chain

periods.activity_title: Decimals in the Real World: Conversions and the Number Line

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions: 70 mm = ___ cm; ___ = 0.9 cm; 134 mm = ___; ___ = 203.6 cm.
Fill in the blanks for cm ↔ m conversions: 36 cm = ___; 50 cm = ___; ___ = 0.89 m; 4 cm = ___; 325 cm = ___; ___ = 2.07 m. Then answer: how many mm in 1 m? Can 1 mm = 1/1000 m?
Draw a number line and locate 1.4 by dividing the unit between 1 and 2 into 10 equal parts. Name all the divisions between 1 and 1.1.
Identify and write the decimal numbers against letters A, B, C, D on the number line segment from 5 to 5.4.
Zero Dilemma: Sonu says 0.2 = 0.20 = 0.200. Zara disagrees. Use the place value table to settle the dispute; then determine which of 4.5, 4.05, 0.405, 4.050, 4.50, 4.005, 04.50 are equal.

homework.description: Fill in the blanks for g ↔ kg conversions: 465 g = ___; 68 g = ___; 1560 g = ___; 704 g = ___; ___ = 0.56 kg; ___ = 2.5 kg.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.64 ("Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions: 70 mm = ___ cm….") and Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.66 ("Fill in the blanks for cm ↔ m conversions….") — students work through both length-conversion tables, deriving each answer from the unit fraction (1 mm = 1/10 cm = 0.1 cm; 1 cm = 1/100 m = 0.01 m).

Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.70 ("Draw a number line and locate 1.4 by dividing the unit between 1 and 2 into 10 equal parts….") and Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.70 ("Identify and write the decimal numbers against letters A, B, C, D on the number line segment from 5 to 5.4.") — students construct and label the number lines, naming each tenth-division between 1 and 1.1.

Math Talk, section 3.6 p.70 ("Zero Dilemma: Sonu says 0.2 = 0.20 = 0.200. Zara disagrees….") — students use a place value table to adjudicate, then classify the seven given expressions into equivalence classes. Class resolves any disagreement about trailing zeros versus leading zeros after the decimal point.
Quick exit check: teacher writes three decimals on the board (e.g., 0.30, 0.03, 3.0) and students write TRUE or FALSE for two equality claims, justifying in one sentence using the place value table.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit covers the final sub-goal of section 3.5 and the opening of section 3.6 together; both are anchored in the 'apply' goal so the unit is coherent. The Zero Dilemma is the most conceptually charged moment — students often accept that trailing zeros are harmless without being able to explain why, so insist they use the place value table as the proof. Homework targets the g ↔ kg conversion, which follows the same logic as the in-class length work.

periods.activity_title: Zooming In, Comparing, and Computing with Decimals

textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the decimal number denoted by '?' in figure (b), where successive zooms of the number line are given (similar to how 4.185 is located in figure (a)).
Which decimal number is greater? (a) 1.23 or 1.32; (b) 3.81 or 13.800; (c) 1.009 or 1.090.
Closest Decimals: (a) which of 0.9, 1.1, 1.01, 1.11 is closest to 1.09; (b) which of 3.56, 3.65, 3.099 is closest to 4; (c) which of 0.8, 0.69, 1.08 is closest to 1.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.75
Figure it Out Q2, section 3.7 p.75

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.71 ("Identify the decimal number denoted by '?' in figure (b), where successive zooms of the number line are given….") — students trace the successive magnification from figure (a) as a model, then independently locate the unknown decimal in figure (b), naming the place value each zoom reveals.

Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.73 ("Which decimal number is greater? (a) 1.23 or 1.32….") and Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.73 ("Closest Decimals: (a) which of 0.9, 1.1, 1.01, 1.11 is closest to 1.09….") — students use left-to-right digit comparison to resolve all three comparisons, then find the closest decimal in each group by computing differences.

Teacher bridges to section 3.7 using the cloth-purchase context (2.7 m + 3.5 m) and shows the column-decimal form alongside the fraction form, making explicit that the same regrouping governs both. Students set up column addition for 75.345 + 86.691 and work through it digit by digit.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.75 ("Find the sums: (a) 5.3 + 2.6; (b) 18 + 8.8….") and Figure it Out Q2, section 3.7 p.75 ("Find the differences: (a) 5.6 – 2.3; (b) 18 – 8.8….") — students complete as many of the eight additions and eight subtractions as possible in the available time, aligning the decimal point in every column layout.

periods.teacher_notes: Comparison by successive digit inspection (left to right, stopping at the first differing digit) is the method the section demonstrates — students who compare digit counts rather than digit values will go wrong on items like 1.009 vs 1.090. For the column arithmetic, the most persistent error is misaligning addends that have different numbers of decimal places (e.g., 0.934 + 0.6); emphasise that the decimal point must be directly above the decimal point.

periods.activity_title: Decimals Matter: Errors, History, and the Whole System

textbook_items_in_class.description: Where else can we see 'non-decimal' numbers written with a decimal-like notation? (The cricket overs and feet-inches examples are given; students generate further instances.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.8 p.78
textbook_items_in_class.description: Convert fractions into decimals: (a) 5/100; (b) 16/1000; (c) 12/10; (d) 254/1000.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 3.8 p.79
textbook_items_in_class.description: Will a decimal number with more digits necessarily be greater than one with fewer digits? Justify with an example.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.8 p.79
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mahi buys 0.25 kg beans, 0.3 kg carrots, 0.5 kg potatoes, 0.2 kg capsicums, 0.05 kg ginger. Calculate total weight.

Evaluate Sonu's claim that the sum of two decimal numbers always lies strictly between (sum of whole-number parts) and (sum of whole-number parts + 2). Verify for 25.936 + 8.202 and for 25.93603259 + 8.202.

time_bands.activity: Teacher narrates the Air Canada Boeing 767 fuel disaster and the Amsterdam housing-benefit overpayment from section 3.8, asking students: what decimal error made each possible? Class identifies the specific misread (pounds for kilograms; cents for euros; 0.5 mg instead of 0.05 mg) and traces exactly how the place value chain was misread in each case.

Math Talk, section 3.8 p.78 ("Where else can we see 'non-decimal' numbers written with a decimal-like notation?….") — students discuss cricket overs and feet-and-inches as pseudo-decimal notations, then generate two further examples of their own, articulating why these are not true decimals.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.8 p.78 ("Convert fractions into decimals: (a) 5/100; (b) 16/1000; (c) 12/10; (d) 254/1000.") and Figure it Out Q6, section 3.8 p.79 ("Will a decimal number with more digits necessarily be greater than one with fewer digits? Justify with an example.") — students complete the conversion task, then write a one-sentence justification with a counter-example for Q6, drawing on place value understanding from decimal notation and the number-line comparison work.

Figure it Out Q7, section 3.8 p.79 ("Mahi buys 0.25 kg beans, 0.3 kg carrots, 0.5 kg potatoes….") — students compute Mahi's total weight using column addition, then turn to Math Talk, section 3.7 p.76 ("Evaluate Sonu's claim that the sum of two decimal numbers always lies strictly between (sum of whole-number parts) and (sum of whole-number parts + 2)….") as a synthesis challenge: they verify the claim for both given sums and decide whether it is always, sometimes, or never true, connecting fractional-part addition back to the place value structure the chapter built from the beginning.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together three threads the chapter developed separately — the necessity of decimal notation (section 3.4), the reality of measurement consequences (section 3.8's disaster vignettes), and the arithmetic of decimal addition (section 3.7). Watch for students who accept Sonu's claim without checking the edge case where the two fractional parts sum to exactly 1; that case falsifies the strict inequality and is a rich closing discussion.

items.prompt: A student places a pencil on a millimetre-ruled scale. The tip of the pencil falls between the 8 cm and 9 cm marks, closer to 8 cm. Which of the following correctly records the pencil's length using tenth-of-a-centimetre notation?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 3/10 cm — the whole-centimetre part (8) is recorded first, then the number of tenth-parts (3) as the fractional part, giving the mixed-number form the section introduces.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the whole-centimetre mark the length has passed, then count the tenth-divisions beyond it and express as a mixed number.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is rounding to the nearest whole centimetre, ignoring the fractional part that the section shows is essential when lengths differ by less than a centimetre.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has concatenated the whole number and the tenths digit without the fractional separator, confusing the mixed number 8 3/10 with the whole number 83.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has recorded only the fractional part and discarded the whole-centimetre reading, losing the magnitude of the measurement entirely.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the screw scenario in section 3.1 and look at how 2 7/10 cm is written there.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the same length as an improper tenth-fraction and explain why both forms describe the same point on the ruler.

exercise.description: Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object of the student's choice using a scale; record the measurements in centimetres using tenth notation as modelled in the section.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly converts the mixed number 5 7/10 into an improper fraction expressed in tenths?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 57/10 — multiply the whole part (5) by 10 to get 50 tenths, then add the 7 tenths, giving 57/10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the whole-number part by 10 and add the numerator: 5 × 10 + 7 = 57, so 57/10.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student reversed the digits of the whole and fractional parts, writing 75 instead of 57 — a positional error in the conversion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student wrote the digits as a simple fraction 5/7 without using the denominator 10 at all, ignoring the tenth-unit entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added the whole number and numerator without multiplying by 10 first: 5 + 7 = 12, giving 12/10 instead of 57/10.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to look back at the pencil-length diagram in section 3.2 that shows 34 one-tenths = 3 full units + 4 tenths.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to convert 13 1/10 and 130/10 and explain in their own words why both represent the same length.

exercise.description: Write lengths of objects (USB cable, and others shown in diagrams) in two ways — as a mixed number and as an improper tenth fraction — and read them aloud.

items.prompt: How many one-hundredths are equal to 3 one-tenths?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the equivalence 1/10 = 10/100: multiply the number of tenths by 10 to find the equivalent number of hundredths.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflated the count of tenths with the count of hundredths, not applying the 10-to-1 ratio between the two units.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student multiplied by 100 instead of 10, confusing how many hundredths make one unit (100) with how many make one tenth (10).
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 10 to the numerator instead of multiplying, an additive error in the place-value conversion.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-examine the folded-paper problem in section 3.3 that shows each tenth splitting into exactly 10 hundredths.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write their own question of the same type — starting from a given number of hundredths and asking how many tenths that equals.

exercise.description: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can the folded-paper length also be stated as 4 units and 45 one-hundredths? Explain.

items.prompt: The digit string '305' could represent three different quantities depending on where the decimal point is placed. Write all three quantities in decimal form and explain, using the place value table, why the same digits produce different values.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 305 (three hundred and five units), 30.5 (thirty units and five tenths), and 3.05 (three units and five hundredths). In each case the digits are the same but occupy different columns in the place value table — hundreds/tens/units, tens/units/tenths, and units/tenths/hundredths respectively — so the value of each digit changes by a factor of ten with each column shift.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place each digit in the place value table (hundreds, tens, units, tenths, hundredths) for each possible decimal point position and read off the value.

inclusivity.support: Talk through your answer with a partner before writing — name the column each digit sits in for one of the three quantities.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one of the digit positions: what if the decimal point produced 0.305? Add this fourth case and explain how it fits the same pattern.

exercise.description: Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator? What ambiguity arises? Show three different quantities that could all be denoted '705' without a positional separator.

items.prompt: Cricket scorecards sometimes write an over as '14.3', meaning 14 complete overs and 3 balls. Explain clearly why this is NOT a decimal number in the mathematical sense, even though it uses a point. In your answer, refer to how a true decimal works and what property the cricket notation lacks.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In the decimal number system, the digit after the point represents tenths — each place is ten times smaller than the one before it. So in a true decimal, '14.3' means 14 and 3 tenths (i.e., 14.3 = 14 + 3/10). In cricket, however, the digit after the point counts balls within an over, and one over has 6 balls — not 10. This means the sub-unit is one-sixth of a whole, not one-tenth. Because the base of the sub-unit is 6 (not 10), the notation does not follow the place-value rule that defines the decimal system. A notation where '14.5' would mean 14 overs and 5 balls — impossibly the same point as '14.3' = 14 overs and 3 balls but also coinciding with '15' if overs ran to base 10 — shows the inconsistency: the system breaks whenever the sub-unit base differs from 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Show that the cricket 'decimal' uses a base-6 sub-unit rather than base-10, violating the defining property of the decimal place value chain.

inclusivity.support: Talk through your reasoning with a partner before writing — start by saying what a true decimal's digit after the point means, then say what the cricket digit after the point means.
inclusivity.challenge: Invent a different context (not cricket) where a decimal-like separator is used but the base is not 10, and explain the same argument for your example.

exercise.description: Where else can we see 'non-decimal' numbers written with a decimal-like notation? (The cricket overs and feet-inches examples are given; students generate further instances.)

items.prompt: A dragonfly's body has three parts: the head is 1 6/10 cm, the thorax is 3 8/10 cm, and the abdomen is 4 9/10 cm. Find the total body length of the dragonfly. Show your working using both the 'units and tenths separately' method and the 'convert to tenths' method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Method 1 (units and tenths separately): Units: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8. Tenths: 6 + 8 + 9 = 23 tenths = 2 units and 3 tenths. Total: 8 + 2 3/10 = 10 3/10 cm. Method 2 (convert to tenths): 16/10 + 38/10 + 49/10 = 103/10 = 10 3/10 cm. Both methods give 10 3/10 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the whole parts and the tenths parts separately, regrouping when the tenths total reaches 10 or more; verify by converting all to improper tenths and adding.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line and mark each part as a jump, landing at the total — see how the jumps pass through a whole number.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the abdomen to 4 5/10 cm. Does that alter which method is easier? Explain why or why not.

exercise.description: Find the total length of a honeybee given head = 2 3/10 units, thorax = 5 4/10 units, abdomen = 7 5/10 units.

items.prompt: A piece of wire measures 18 3/10 7/100 units. A second piece measures 9 6/10 8/100 units. Find the difference in their lengths. Show your working using column decomposition (units, tenths, hundredths) and verify by converting both lengths to hundredths.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Method 1 (column): Hundredths: 7 – 8 requires regrouping — borrow 1 tenth (= 10 hundredths): 17 – 8 = 9 hundredths; tenths: (3 – 1) – 6 requires regrouping — borrow 1 unit (= 10 tenths): (12 – 1) – 6 = 5 tenths; units: (18 – 1) – 9 = 8. Result: 8 5/10 9/100. Method 2 (convert): 18 3/10 7/100 = 1837/100; 9 6/10 8/100 = 968/100; 1837 – 968 = 869; 869/100 = 8 69/100 = 8 6/10 9/100. Both give 8 6/10 9/100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align units, tenths, and hundredths in columns; regroup across place values as needed, then verify by converting to hundredths and subtracting the whole numbers.

inclusivity.support: Set up the column layout on squared paper, writing one digit per square, and label the columns before subtracting.
inclusivity.challenge: Swap the two lengths and compute the difference in the other direction — explain why the regrouping steps change.

exercise.description: Solve by converting to hundredths: find the difference 25 9/10 – 6 4/10 7/100; then find 15 3/10 4/100 – 2 6/10 8/100 and observe structural similarity with whole-number column subtraction 653 – 268.

items.prompt: A ribbon is 245 mm long. Express this length in centimetres and in metres, writing both answers in decimal form. Show the conversion step for each.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the unit fraction 1 mm = 0.1 cm to convert to centimetres, then 1 cm = 0.01 m to convert to metres, multiplying at each step.

inclusivity.support: Start from the known fact 1 cm = 10 mm, rewrite it as 1 mm = 1/10 cm, and then express 1/10 as a decimal before multiplying.
inclusivity.challenge: If a second ribbon is 0.38 m long, express that length in centimetres and in millimetres, and compare the two ribbons' lengths.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions: 70 mm = ___ cm; ___ = 0.9 cm; 134 mm = ___; ___ = 203.6 cm.

items.prompt: A student draws a number line from 3 to 4 and divides it into 10 equal parts. She then zooms into the interval between 3.2 and 3.3 and divides that into 10 equal parts. Which of the four decimals 3.27, 3.72, 3.207, and 3.270 can she locate on her zoomed number line, and which is greatest? Show left-to-right digit comparison to justify your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3.27 and 3.270 are equal (trailing zero does not change value) and both lie in the interval 3.2–3.3, so both can be located on the zoomed number line at the 7th subdivision after 3.2. 3.207 also lies in 3.2–3.3 (it is between 3.20 and 3.21) and can be located. 3.72 lies between 3.7 and 3.8 and cannot be located on a zoom of 3.2–3.3. Comparison by left-to-right digits: all four share '3' in the units place. Moving to tenths: 3.72 has 7 tenths vs 2 tenths for the others — so 3.72 is greatest. Among 3.27, 3.270, and 3.207: units equal (3), tenths equal (2), hundredths: 7 vs 7 vs 0 — so 3.27 = 3.270 > 3.207.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare digits left to right, stopping at the first differing digit; apply the trailing-zero rule to confirm 3.27 = 3.270.

inclusivity.support: Draw the number line from 3 to 4 on squared paper, mark the ten subdivisions, and then draw the zoom box around 3.2–3.3 before trying to place the numbers.
inclusivity.challenge: What is the decimal number exactly halfway between 3.207 and 3.27? Explain how you found it using the number line zoom idea.

exercise.description: Identify the decimal number denoted by '?' in figure (b), where successive zooms of the number line are given (similar to how 4.185 is located in figure (a)).

items.prompt: A tailor uses 4.85 m of cloth for a kurta and 2.6 m for matching trousers. She started with a 10 m roll. How much cloth remains? Show column addition and column subtraction with the decimal point aligned.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1 — total cloth used: 4.85 + 2.60 (writing 2.6 as 2.60 to align columns). Hundredths: 5 + 0 = 5. Tenths: 8 + 6 = 14; write 4, carry 1. Units: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. Total = 7.45 m. Step 2 — cloth remaining: 10.00 – 7.45. Hundredths: 0 – 5 requires regrouping. Tenths: (10 – 1) – 4 = 5 (after borrowing from units). Units: 9 – 7 = 2. Tens: 1 – 0 = 1. Wait — 10.00 – 7.45: units column: 0 – 5 requires borrowing, giving 10 – 5 = 5 hundredths; tenths: (9 – 1) – 4 = 4 after two layers of regrouping; units: 2 – 7 requires borrowing, giving 12 – 7 = 3 (actually: 10.00 – 7.45: work column by column: hundredths 0–5 borrow: 10–5=5; tenths (9 carry)–4=5 but need to recheck: 10.00 = 9 units 9 tenths 10 hundredths after one borrow, then 9 units 10 tenths after second borrow is wrong — careful: 10.00 hundredths column: borrow from tenths (tenths becomes 9, hundredths becomes 10): 10–5=5; tenths column 9–4=5 but units now 9: 9–7=2; tens 1–0=1. Result: 10.00 – 7.45 = 2.55 m. Cloth remaining = 2.55 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the two cloth lengths in column form (aligning decimal points), then subtract the total from 10.00 using column subtraction with regrouping.

inclusivity.support: Write 2.6 as 2.60 and 10 as 10.00 before setting up any column — the zeros make the alignment visible and reduce regrouping errors.
inclusivity.challenge: If the tailor also needed 1.375 m for a dupatta from the same roll, how much cloth would be left? Extend your column working to include the third piece.
